name: The four yogas (mantra, laya, haṭha, rāja)

definitions.definition: The haṭha texts' classification of yoga into mantrayoga (lowest), layayoga, haṭhayoga and rājayoga (highest) — first in the Dattātreyayogaśāstra (9), then the Amaraughaprabodha, Śiva Saṃhitā (5.9) and others; the Śiva Saṃhitā assigns them to four grades of aspirant; the Yogabīja and Haṭharatnāvalī call them one 'great yoga'. The DYŚ also says the eight-limbed yoga of Yājñavalkya and the haṭha of Kapila differ in practice, not in fruit.

name: The four stages of yoga (ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya, niṣpatti)

definitions.definition: Four stages 'in all yogas' (HYP 4.69), first taught in the Amṛtasiddhi: in the HYP they are marked by the piercing of the three knots and by the inner sounds (4.70–77); in the DYŚ by signs of breath-mastery, the union of prāṇa and apāna, the element-concentrations and rājayoga (81–147); in the Śiva Saṃhitā by bodily signs, the seeing of karma's 'three peaks' and liberation while living.

relations.note: in the HYP the first, second and fourth stages coincide with the piercing of the three knots

definitions.definition: In the haṭha texts bindu is the vital essence (semen; with rajas in women), identified with the moon and the nectar in the head; life depends on it and its fall is death (Amṛtasiddhi; HYP 3.88); cosmologically bindu is Śiva and rajas Śakti (SS 1.92); Śiva's nature is nāda, bindu and kalā (HYP 4.1).

The coiled power at the base of the central channel, blocking its mouth; the support of all yoga (HYP 3.1); awakened by the guru's grace (3.2) and by breath, locks and mudrās (3.5, 3.66–69) she straightens like a struck snake, pierces the knots and lotuses and the mind becomes supportless; for yogins she is liberation, for fools bondage (3.107). The GŚ says she is coiled eightfold, the ṢCN three and a half times; the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa describes her ascent through six centres to union with Paramaśiva.

The knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra, pierced when kuṇḍalinī awakens (HYP 3.2) and, in the nāda-stages, at ārambha, ghaṭa and niṣpatti respectively (4.70–77); bhastrikā retention is said to break them (2.67).

The haṭha texts count 72,000 channels arising from the bulb (GŚ 16; HYP 1.39, 4.18) — or 350,000 (SS 2.13) — with ten (GŚ 17–22) or fourteen (SS 2.13) principal and three chief: iḍā, piṅgalā and suṣumnā; they must be purified before the breath can enter the middle (HYP 2.4–5); only suṣumnā matters, the rest are 'useless' (HYP 4.18).

Five principal breaths (prāṇa in the heart, apāna at the anus, samāna at the navel, udāna in the throat, vyāna throughout) and five minor ones (nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, dhanañjaya) causing belching, blinking, hunger, yawning and hiccup (SS 3.4–8); they move in the channels as the living soul (GŚ 24–25).

The haṭha texts give different body-maps: six centres (ādhāra/mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddha, ājñā) with the thousand-petalled lotus above (GŚ 10–15, 60–62, 78–85; ṢCN); the Nāth scheme of six (or nine) centres, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids (Vivekamārtaṇḍa; Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati); the Śiva Saṃhitā's centres with Kailāsa, the sahasrāra, 'outside the body called brahmāṇḍa' (5.151); the GS's twelve-petalled lotus within the thousand-petalled where the guru is meditated on. Numbers, petals, letters and deities differ between texts.

In Pūrṇānanda's Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa (1577) the six centres are strung on the brahmanāḍī within citriṇī, vajrā and suṣumnā: mūlādhāra (4 petals, earth, LAṂ, Brahmā, Ḍākinī), svādhiṣṭhāna (6, water, VAṂ, Viṣṇu), maṇipūra (10, fire, RAṂ, Rudra), anāhata (12, air, YAṂ, Īśa), viśuddha (16, space, HAṂ, Sadāśiva), ājñā (2, mind, praṇava, Śambhu), and the thousand-petalled lotus with Paramaśiva above.

relations.note: six-centre maps vs the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati's nine; not reconciled in the texts themselves

definitions.definition: In the haṭha body-map the three targets (inner, outer, middle) are among the things the yogin must know in his own body (Vivekamārtaṇḍa family); śāmbhavī mudrā is attention on an inner target with the gaze outward (HYP 4.36).
The five voids of the Nāth body-map that the yogin must know in his own body (Vivekamārtaṇḍa family); the HYP's khecarī is 'in the space-wheel (vyomacakra) between sun and moon' (4.45).

relations.note: U04 and U21 created two ids for the same list; flagged for the merge

name: Unmanī / manonmanī — the state beyond mind

definitions.definition: The state beyond mind: it cannot arise while the channels are impure (HYP 2.4); it is the steadiness of mind when breath moves in the middle (2.42); a synonym of samādhi and rājayoga (4.3–4); through it duality is not perceived (4.61) and the body becomes like a log (4.106); it sprouts from tattva, haṭha and detachment (4.104).

relations.standpoint: the HYP's list of synonyms of samādhi

definitions.definition: The inner (unstruck) sound heard in the purified suṣumnā; the HYP makes attention to it the chief of the layas (4.66), maps its sounds onto the four stages (4.69–77) and says whatever is heard as nāda is śakti and the soundless is the supreme Brahman (4.101–102); Śiva is 'of the nature of nāda, bindu and kalā' (4.1).

In the haṭha corpus: 'tāraka', which those deluded by Āgamas, Vedas and logic do not know (HYP 4.40), and the mindless (amanaska) state — a synonym of samādhi (4.4) and the goal of the Amanaska, reached effortlessly by the guru's grace (Amanaska 2).

In the haṭha texts a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4): the yogin in samādhi, not devoured by time nor bound by karma, knowing neither heat nor cold, 'remaining in waking as if asleep, without breath', is liberated (4.106–112); nirguṇa meditation and samādhi make one jīvanmukta, who may leave the body at will or roam with powers (DYŚ 111–118); SS 3.67 speaks of the calm jīvanmukta at niṣpatti.
In HYP 4.62 kaivalya is what remains when the mind dissolves by abandoning the knowable.
The haṭha texts use 'turyā/turya' as a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4) and locate it between the brows, 'the place of Śiva', where mind dissolves and time is not (4.48).

The DYŚ lists the powers that arise in the ghaṭa stage (clairaudience, clairvoyance, speed, perfect speech, invisibility, alchemy, flight) and says they are obstacles to the great accomplishment: the yogin should not delight in them, should hide them and live as if dull or deaf, lest disciples crowd round and he forget his practice (84–95). The HYP nonetheless promises the eight powers from the mudrās (3.8, 3.130).

The interpolated HYP verses (with 1.17) and the Yoga Yājñavalkya list ten restraints (non-harming, truth, non-stealing, continence, forbearance, fortitude, compassion, straightforwardness, moderate diet, purity) and ten observances; the DYŚ says moderate eating is chief among the yamas and non-harming among the niyamas (30); the SS gives its own lists of things to avoid and to follow (3.33, 3.35).

The haṭha compendia include the signs of approaching death: the Haṭhatattvakaumudī's chapter on kālavañcana; the Śiva Svarodaya's prognostication from the breath; the Śiva Saṃhitā's gazing at one's shadow-image in the sky (seeing it whole means long life).

The Yogabīja teaches that the body must be ripened in the fire of yoga; the unripe body, even of a knower, remains subject to karma and rebirth (compare GS 1.8: the body as an unbaked pot to be fired by yoga).

The HYP gives its own sequence: first ocean, thunder, kettledrum and cymbals; in the middle drum, conch, bell and horn; at the end tinkling bells, flute, vīṇā and bee (4.84–86), and one sound for each stage (4.70–77).

name: The body as microcosm (piṇḍa and brahmāṇḍa)

definitions.definition: The Śiva Saṃhitā places Meru, the continents, rivers, oceans, seers, stars, planets, sacred fords and their deities, sun and moon and the elements within the body; 'he who knows this is a yogin' (2.1–5); the body is called brahmāṇḍa (1.91).
Jālandhara 'binds the sixteen supports' (HYP 3.73); the Vivekamārtaṇḍa family lists them among what the yogin must know in his own body; the Haṭhatattvakaumudī devotes a chapter to them.

name: Rājayoga as the goal and its synonyms

definitions.definition: Haṭha is taught solely for rājayoga (HYP 1.2), a stairway to it (1.1); rājayoga is one of sixteen names of samādhi: rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī, manonmanī, amaratva, laya, tattva, śūnyāśūnya, paraṃ padam, amanaska, advaita, nirālamba, nirañjana, jīvanmukti, sahajā, turyā (4.3–4); samādhi is the union of self and mind, the sameness when breath and mind are dissolved, the union of jīvātman and paramātman (4.5–7); the GS equates rājayoga, samādhi, unmanī and the natural state (7.17); the Jyotsnā identifies rājayoga with asamprajñāta yoga.

relations.note: an identification made by the commentator, not by the root text

definitions.definition: The haṭha texts promise the conquest of time/death: the Siddhas 'broke the staff of time' (HYP 1.9); breath held, fear of death is gone (2.39–40); when kuṇḍalinī wakes, death is cheated (3.3); mudrās grant 'cheating of time' (3.130); suṣumnā devours time (4.17); the one established in rājayoga cheats time (4.103); the Haṭhatattvakaumudī has a chapter on it.

name: Perfection of the body and immortality (kāya-siddhi, amaratva)

definitions.definition: In the haṭha texts bodily perfection (dehasiddhi, HYP 3.103) and immortality (amaratva, a synonym of samādhi, 4.3) are fruits of retaining bindu and nectar; the DYŚ's perfected yogin may keep his body and roam the worlds at will (115–118); the Yogabīja's 'ripe body'.

name: Sun, moon and fire in the body

definitions.definition: The moon in the head (or at the palate) rains nectar; the sun/fire at the navel swallows it, and so the body ages and dies (HYP 3.77; GŚ 55–58; SS 2.6–12; Amṛtasiddhi); iḍā is the moon and left, piṅgalā the sun and right; sun and moon create time, which suṣumnā devours (HYP 4.17); haṭha is the union of ha (sun) and ṭha (moon) (Yogabīja; Jyotsnā). The Śiva Svarodaya reads the alternation of the nostrils as the flow of moon and sun.

In the haṭha texts the nectar dripping from the moon in the head is saved from the sun's fire by jālandhara, viparītakaraṇī and khecarī (HYP 3.70–79; DYŚ 126–128) and drunk by the yogin with the tongue turned back; the body filled with it is not abandoned by the soul (HYP 3.46; GŚ 66); its 'liquor' (amaravāruṇī) is the true meaning of transgressive drinking (HYP 3.47–49).

The haṭha texts make the preservation of bindu central: 'death by the fall of bindu, life by holding bindu' (HYP 3.88; DYŚ 143); bindu depends on mind, life on bindu (HYP 3.90); steadiness of mind makes breath and bindu steady (4.28); loss of bindu through women is the great danger of the ghaṭa stage (DYŚ 77–80); khecarī and vajrolī (restricted) are taught to retain or draw it up.

In the HYP laya is the lord of the breath, resting on nāda (4.29); 'the forgetting of objects because latent impressions do not arise' (4.34); an indescribable bliss, whether or not it is called liberation (4.30–32); Ādinātha taught a crore and a quarter kinds (4.66; DYŚ: eight crore saṅketas, 14–24).

In the HYP suṣumnā is 'the path of the void' (3.4); the breath dissolves in the void when śakti wakes (4.10–12); the nāda stages pass through śūnya, atiśūnya and mahāśūnya (4.70–75); 'empty within, empty without, like a pot in space; full within, full without, like a pot in the ocean' (4.56); samādhi is 'void and not void' (śūnyāśūnya, 4.3).

The natural state (sahajāvasthā), a synonym of samādhi (HYP 4.4), which arises spontaneously when śakti has awakened and action is abandoned (4.11) but is hard to reach without a true guru's compassion (4.9); in paricaya 'natural bliss' arises (4.75); GS 7.17 equates it with rājayoga and unmanī.
The sameness (samarasatva) when breath is exhausted and mind dissolved — a definition of samādhi (HYP 4.6; GŚ 94).

name: Secrecy and the testing of the disciple

definitions.definition: Haṭha must be kept secret — potent when hidden, impotent when revealed (HYP 1.11); the mudrās like a jewel box, told to no one (3.9, 3.18; GS 3.5); the yoga śāstra only for a true devotee (SS 1.19); vajrolī only for one as dear as one's life (DYŚ 137); powers never to be displayed (DYŚ 92–93); the Jyotsnā lists who may and may not receive haṭha.

The texts explain the name in two ways: as 'force' — kuṇḍalinī rises 'by force' (haṭhāt, HYP 3.111) and is to be seized 'by force' (3.109) — and as the union of 'ha', the sun, and 'ṭha', the moon (Yogabīja; quoted by the Jyotsnā as from the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati), i.e. of prāṇa and apāna in breath-control. The Śārṅgadhara Paddhati distinguishes Gorakṣa's haṭha from that of Mṛkaṇḍu's son.

name: Haṭha and rājayoga need each other

definitions.definition: Without haṭha rājayoga does not succeed and without rājayoga haṭha does not; both are practised to completion (HYP 2.76; SS 5.181); those who practise only haṭha without knowing rājayoga labour without fruit (HYP 4.79); all haṭha and laya methods are for rājayoga (4.103); tattva is the seed, haṭha the field, detachment the water (4.104).

relations.note: the Amanaska rejects laborious haṭha methods as means to the mindless state; see dsp:amanaska-critique-of-hatha

definitions.definition: The middle channel between iḍā and piṅgalā, blocked by kuṇḍalinī and by impurities; when purified and opened the breath enters it, the mind becomes steady (manonmanī) and time is 'devoured' (HYP 2.41–42, 3.3, 4.17); synonyms: śūnyapadavī, brahmarandhra, mahāpatha, śmaśāna, śāmbhavī, madhyamārga (3.4); within it lie vajrā, citriṇī and the brahmanāḍī (SS 2.18; ṢCN 1–2).

name: The bond of mind and breath

definitions.definition: Mind and breath are mixed like milk and water: when breath moves mind moves, when breath is still mind is still (HYP 2.2); who binds the one binds the other; the mind has two causes, latent impressions and breath, and when one is destroyed both are (4.21–25); the mind is lord of the senses, breath lord of the mind, laya lord of breath (4.29); knowledge cannot arise while breath lives and mind is not dead (4.15); the living soul is pulled up and down by prāṇa and apāna (GŚ 26–29).

name: The guru in the haṭha texts

definitions.definition: Haṭha is learned 'by the path taught by the guru' (HYP 1.14, 2.1); kuṇḍalinī wakes by the guru's grace (3.2); viparītakaraṇī is known from the guru's instruction 'not from ten million śāstras' (3.78–79); the one who gives traditional instruction in the mudrās is the Lord himself (3.129); knowledge, liberation and the natural state are hard to obtain without a true guru's compassion (4.8–9); knowledge from the guru's mouth is potent, otherwise fruitless (SS 3.11); samādhi comes through the guru's grace and devotion to him (GS 7.1).

relations.note: the same teaching seen in the texts and in the living Nāth order (U21)
relations.standpoint: haṭha manuals vs the Nāth order

name: The place and hut for yoga

definitions.definition: The haṭha yogin lives alone in a small hut in a righteous, prosperous and peaceful kingdom, free of rock, fire and water around, with a small door, no holes, smeared with cow-dung, walled, with a well (HYP 1.12–14; GS 5.5–7); not in a distant land, forest, capital or crowd (GS 5.3–4); begin in spring or autumn, not in winter, summer or the rains (GS 5.8–9).

name: Moderate diet (mitāhāra) in the haṭha texts

definitions.definition: Moderate diet is smooth, sweet food eaten to please Śiva, leaving a quarter of the stomach empty (HYP 1.58); the chief of the yamas (HYP 1.38; DYŚ 30); lists of wholesome and unwholesome foods (HYP 1.59–63; GS 5.17–25; DYŚ 64–66); without it yoga brings disease (GS 5.16).

name: What destroys and what promotes yoga (HYP 1.15–16)

definitions.definition: Six things destroy yoga — overeating, overexertion, too much talk, clinging to rules, company of people, unsteadiness — and six bring success — enthusiasm, boldness, patience, knowledge of truth, determination, abandoning company.

The texts say success comes to anyone who practises — young, old, sick or weak (HYP 1.64; DYŚ 37) — whatever his sect: brāhmaṇa, śramaṇa, Buddhist, Jain, Kāpālika or materialist (DYŚ 38); nāda is for the dull too (HYP 4.65, 4.80); householders can succeed (SS 5.186, 5.210–212); but some practices succeed only for the virtuous and envy-free (HYP 3.95); the SS grades aspirants and assigns them yogas; the Jyotsnā holds the dispassionate alone properly eligible and lists who may receive haṭha.

relations.note: universal eligibility by practice vs graded fitness; see the interpretation log (P4-stage)

definitions.definition: Mild (mṛdu) → mantrayoga, success in twelve years; middling (madhya) → layayoga; strong (adhimātra) → haṭhayoga with its limbs, six years; strongest (adhimātratama) → all the yogas, three years (SS 5.10–14; DYŚ 12 for the mild).

name: The seven means of the yoga of the pot (Gheraṇḍa)

definitions.definition: Purification (by the six acts), firmness (posture), steadiness (mudrā), calm (withdrawal), lightness (breath-control), direct perception of the self (meditation), non-attachment and liberation (samādhi) (GS 1.9–11).

Gross meditation on a form (the chosen deity or the guru), meditation on light (kuṇḍalinī as a flame, the navel sun, the praṇava-light between the brows) and subtle meditation on bindu/kuṇḍalinī by śāmbhavī; each is vastly superior to the one before (GS 6.1–22).
Through śāmbhavī (meditation), bhrāmarī (nāda), khecarī (bliss of taste) and yonimudrā (laya), through devotion, and through the swoon of the mind — six-fold rājayoga (GS 7.5–16).

name: The ten mudrās of the Haṭhapradīpikā

definitions.definition: Mahāmudrā, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, uḍḍiyāna, mūlabandha, jālandhara, viparītakaraṇī, vajrolī and śakticālana — taught by Ādinātha, destroying old age and death, to be kept secret (HYP 3.6–9, 3.128); a closely similar set in DYŚ 27–29.

name: The twenty-five mudrās of the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā

definitions.definition: GS 3.1–3 lists twenty-five: mahāmudrā, nabhomudrā, uḍḍīyāna, jālandhara, mūlabandha, mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, viparītakaraṇī, yoni, vajrolī, śakticālanī, tāḍāgī, māṇḍukī, śāmbhavī, the five dhāraṇās, aśvinī, pāśinī, kākī, mātaṅgī and bhujaṅginī.

Śiva taught eighty-four postures (HYP 1.33; GŚ 6; HR; Jogapradīpikā) — or as many as there are species, 8,400,000, of which 84 are distinguished and 32 useful for mortals (GS 2.1–2); of these the texts select four (HYP 1.34), two (GŚ 7) or thirty-two (GS 2.3–6).

name: The thirty-two postures of the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā

definitions.definition: The list of GS 2.3–6.

name: The doctrine of the cleansing acts

definitions.definition: The HYP prescribes the six acts only for those with excess fat or phlegm, whose humours are unbalanced (2.21), keeps them secret (2.23), and reports that some teachers hold breath-control alone sufficient (2.37); the GS makes the acts the first of its seven means for everyone (1.9–12); the Haṭharatnāvalī and Haṭhatattvakaumudī count eight.

HYP 2.44: sūryabhedana, ujjāyī, sītkārī, śītalī, bhastrikā, bhrāmarī, mūrcchā, plāvinī (with sahita and kevala as the two kinds of retention, 2.71); GS 5.47: sahita, sūryabheda, ujjāyī, śītalī, bhastrikā, bhrāmarī, mūrcchā, kevalī. RESTRICTED as to method and measures.

The Śiva Svarodaya's teaching that the breath flows by turns through the left (moon), right (sun) or both (suṣumnā) nostrils, that actions should match the flow, that suṣumnā's flow suits only meditation, and that the flow foretells events and death.

name: The five elements in the breath

definitions.definition: In each nostril-flow the five elements arise in turn, recognized by the breath's length, direction, colour and taste (Śiva Svarodaya).

HYP 1.5–8 names some thirty-three great Siddhas, beginning with Ādinātha, Matsyendra, Śābara, Ānandabhairava, Cauraṅgī, Mīna, Gorakṣa and Virūpākṣa and ending with Kāpālika, who by haṭha broke the staff of time and roam the universe (1.9). Several names recur in the Buddhist list of eighty-four Mahāsiddhas and in Nāth lists (see U21, U49).

relations.note: overlapping lists, not identical; U49 compares the Nāth and Buddhist lists

name: Transgressive language given a yogic sense

definitions.definition: The HYP takes Kaula-sounding injunctions — eat cow's flesh, drink the liquor of the immortals, seize the young widow between Gaṅgā and Yamunā, worship the liṅga neither by day nor by night — and explains them as yogic acts: the tongue entering the palate, the moon's nectar, kuṇḍalinī between iḍā and piṅgalā, restraint of sun and moon (3.47–49, 3.109–110, 4.42).

The HYP compares mind and mercury: both unsteady by nature; bound, they accomplish everything (4.26–27); nāda 'calcines' the mercury of the mind (4.96). An analogy from rasaśāstra; no alchemical procedure is taught.

name: The four yogas as one great yoga

definitions.definition: The Yogabīja and the Haṭharatnāvalī teach that mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja are aspects of one 'great yoga' (mahāyoga), against a strict hierarchy of lower and higher yogas.

name: Practice, not garb or learning, is the cause of success

definitions.definition: Success comes from practice alone, not from reading scriptures, wearing an ascetic's garb or talking about yoga (HYP 1.65–66; DYŚ 39–46, which names shaven heads, staffs, ochre robes, matted locks, ash and sectarian mantras as no cause of success and condemns garb-wearers who deceive for 'penis and belly').

Sweat, then trembling, then the breath reaching its place (HYP 2.12); sweat, trembling of the spine, rising from the ground (GS 5.57); sweat, trembling, hopping like a frog, levitation, scant sleep and excreta, freedom from disease, great strength (SS 3.40–46; DYŚ 69–76).

name: The dangers of forcing (the texts' own warnings)

definitions.definition: The breath is to be tamed gradually like a lion, elephant or tiger, otherwise it kills the practitioner (HYP 2.15); improper practice causes hiccup, asthma, cough, pains of head, ears and eyes (2.16–17); release, fill and hold it 'skilfully' (2.18); draw and release it slowly, never holding too long (GŚ 51); beginning at the wrong season or without moderate diet brings disease (GS 5.8–9, 5.16); viparītakaraṇī needs ample food or the fire burns the body (HYP 3.80–81); khecarī's preparation only under a guru (Khecarīvidyā).

The perfected yogin may leave the body at will and dissolve in the supreme Brahman, or keep it (DYŚ 115–118); the Haṭhatattvakaumudī has a chapter on a breath practice for utkrānti. RESTRICTED: recorded as teaching only; no method.

name: Samādhi as the union of the individual and supreme self

definitions.definition: The haṭha texts describe the self in samādhi as the union of jīvātman and paramātman (HYP 4.7; DYŚ 82, 114), 'separating mind from body and uniting it with the supreme self' (GS 7.3) — 'I am Brahman, being-consciousness-bliss' (GS 7.4); the Śiva Saṃhitā's one eternal knowledge (1.1). The metaphysics is borrowed from Advaita; the practice texts do not argue it.

name: Karma and its uprooting in the haṭha texts

definitions.definition: The body arises from good and bad deeds and turns the soul through birth and death like a water-wheel (GS 1.6–7); when breath flows in suṣumnā and mind enters the void the yogin uproots all karma (HYP 4.12); the yogin in samādhi is not bound by karma (4.108); at niṣpatti the seeds of beginningless karma are crossed (SS 3.66); in paricaya he sees the 'three peaks' of his karma (SS 3.61).
